title: Record the declared purpose of each automated client before setting policy
statement: Crawler policy is written from a maintained list of automated clients, where each entry names the token the client sends, the operator running it, the purpose that operator publishes for it, and the decision taken, so no directive is written against a token whose purpose nobody established.
rationale: Operators run several tokens for unrelated purposes, so a policy written from a token name alone tends to block search discovery while intending to block model training.
implementation: Keep the list beside the robots file so the two are edited together, record where each purpose was read from and on what date, and revisit an entry when the operator's documentation changes rather than when traffic changes.

verification.method: Compare the tokens named in the served robots file against the maintained list and report any token present in one but absent from the other.

caution: The cited documentation establishes which tokens exist and what each is for. Maintaining an inventory of them is this registry's synthesis rather than a published requirement, which is why the record is tier B.

title: Set training access policy separately from search indexing policy
statement: The directive governing model-training access occupies its own group, and the operator's search-indexing token keeps whatever access it previously had, so declining training use does not withdraw the site from search.
rationale: A single operator uses distinct tokens for indexing and for training, and a rule aimed at the wrong one removes the site from results while leaving training access untouched.
implementation: Give the training token its own group with its own rules rather than adding it to the group that governs the indexing token, then confirm the indexing token still resolves to the access it had beforehand.

verification.method: Evaluate the served robots file for the training token and for the indexing token independently, confirming the result for the indexing token is unchanged by the training rule.

caution: Declining training access is a licensing decision rather than a discoverability one. This record requires only that the two decisions be expressed independently, and recommends neither answer.

title: Distinguish retrieval tokens from training tokens for one operator
statement: Where an operator publishes one token for gathering training data and another for answering a live question, each token receives its own decision, because permitting the answering path and declining the collection path are different choices.
rationale: Treating an operator as a single actor collapses two independent decisions into one, so a site that wants to be quotable in answers can end up excluded from them purely in order to decline training.
implementation: Read the operator's published token list and write one group per purpose, naming only tokens that list documents. A token nobody documents gets no rule, since a rule against a name that is never sent has no effect.

verification.method: Evaluate the served robots file once per documented token for the operator and record the access decision each one resolves to.

caution: Token names and stated purposes change without notice, and a token withdrawn from an operator's documentation may still appear in logs. The review interval is short for that reason, and no claim is made here about what an operator does with content it retrieves.

title: Allow user-triggered fetching of pages the reader can already open
statement: A fetch made because a person asked an assistant to read a specific public URL is permitted for pages that person could open in a browser, and is not caught by the rule written to govern bulk collection.
rationale: Blocking this path denies a reader access to a page they were already entitled to read, and the request exists because they asked for it rather than because a crawler discovered the URL.
implementation: Give the user-triggered token an allow rule scoped to the paths a signed-out reader can reach, and leave paths behind authentication governed by authentication rather than by this rule.

verification.method: Evaluate the served robots file for each documented user-triggered token against one public path and one authenticated path, confirming the public path is permitted while the authenticated path stays protected.

caution: The operator documentation establishes that these tokens exist and are sent on behalf of a person, which supports the token list rather than the recommendation itself, so this record is tier B. Whether to permit the fetch is a policy choice, and permitting it creates no obligation on the assistant to cite the page.

title: Enforce one crawler policy across robots.txt and the edge
statement: The decision expressed in the robots file is the decision the perimeter enforces, so a token the file permits is not rate-limited into failure, challenged, or refused by a rule maintained separately at the edge.
rationale: Two independently maintained policies drift apart, and the one that decides the outcome is the perimeter rule rather than the file the operator reads and believes to be in force.
implementation: Derive the perimeter rules from the same list the robots file is written from, and where the perimeter must throttle a permitted token, throttle it to a rate that still completes rather than to a refusal.

verification.method: Request a sample of public paths under each documented token and compare the status returned through the perimeter against the decision the robots file expresses for that token.

title: Confirm client identity by reverse DNS rather than the user-agent string
statement: Where a rule grants access on the basis of which client is asking, that identity is confirmed by a reverse lookup on the requesting address followed by a forward lookup, or by matching a published address range, because the token itself is chosen by whoever sends it.
rationale: Any client can send any token, so a rule that trusts the string grants whatever that rule grants to anyone who copies it out of a log.
implementation: Confirm identity at the point where the decision is made, cache the outcome briefly rather than resolving per request, and fail closed to the policy for unidentified clients instead of the policy for the claimed one.

verification.method: Send a request carrying a privileged token from an address outside the operator's published ranges and confirm it receives the unidentified-client policy.

caution: Not every operator publishes address ranges or supports a reverse lookup. Where neither exists the identity cannot be confirmed at all, and the honest response is to treat the token as unverified rather than to trust it.

title: Give a robots.txt group only to a token a request actually sends
statement: A robots.txt group naming an automated client is written only for a token that client sends as an HTTP user-agent. A product-level control token, which an operator applies to traffic its existing user agents already generate, is never given a group, because no request can match one.
rationale: Google states that Google-Extended is not a separate crawler identity but an opt-out applied to data collected by the user agents already visiting the site, and Apple documents Applebot-Extended the same way. A group written for such a token matches nothing on the wire, so the file records an intent it does not enforce, and reading it as evidence that the traffic was refused draws the opposite conclusion from the one that holds.
implementation: Look each named token up in the operator's own documentation before writing a group for it, and record the purpose it is documented as serving. Where the documentation describes a control rather than a fetcher, express the decision in the operator's own surface and remove the group from robots.txt. Never treat a group for such a token as proof that the traffic was blocked.

verification.method: Compare every User-agent group in robots.txt against the tokens the named operator documents, and confirm each group names a fetcher that sends that string.
